text:
**Yes, at about $449-$499 it's a good buy for AC-heavy use like outages, camping and power tools. At higher prices, or if weight matters, newer models are probably better.**

**Why it's worth it**
- **Real capacity is good.** Independent tests measured roughly 950-1,030 Wh usable out of the rated 1,152 Wh, or 82-90% ([Watt Power Station](https://wattpowerstation.com/power-stations/bluetti-ac180/), [PCWorld](https://www.pcworld.com/article/1966571/bluetti-ac180-power-station-review.html)).
- **It handles heavy loads.** It puts out 1,800 W continuous. The 2,700 W "Power Lifting" mode is for resistive loads like heaters and kettles only ([Best Batteries](https://us.best-batteries.com/reviews/bluetti-ac180/)).
- **The battery should last.** It uses LiFePO4 cells rated for 3,500+ cycles, with a 5-year warranty ([BLUETTI](https://www.bluettipower.com/products/ac180?variant=44099774480603)).
- **It charges fast.** About 80% in 45 minutes from the wall, and up to 500 W of solar input.
- **The price is reasonable.** BLUETTI lists it at $499. Other sources show $449 (including on Amazon) ([iTechGuides](https://www.itechguides.com/bluetti-ac180-power-station-review-excellent-ac-efficiency-but-heavy-and-less-impressive-over-dc/)), so compare before buying.

**Downsides**
- **It's heavy.** At about 36 lb it's weighty for 1.15 kWh. OutdoorGearLab scored it 66 overall, citing a poor power-to-weight ratio and a noisy fan ([OutdoorGearLab](https://www.outdoorgearlab.com/reviews/camping-and-hiking/power-station/bluetti-ac180)).
- **DC efficiency is weak.** PCWorld measured only about 71% on a USB-style load, so it's best for AC devices ([iTechGuides](https://www.itechguides.com/bluetti-ac180-power-station-review-excellent-ac-efficiency-but-heavy-and-less-impressive-over-dc/)).
- **It wastes power on small loads.** Outdoor Life measured only 54% of rated capacity at a ~34 W load, which matters for a CPAP or overnight fridge ([Watt Power Station](https://wattpowerstation.com/power-stations/bluetti-ac180/)).
- **Expansion is murky.** BLUETTI's page advertises B80/B230/B300 batteries, but they only work as a top-up in Power Bank Mode. One review says it isn't truly expandable ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/answers/bluetti-ac180-review-price-2026-battery-capacity-limitations-review)).
- **It's being phased out.** OutdoorGearLab says the successor is the Elite 100 V2 (1,024 Wh, 25 lb, quieter, faster charging), and calls it a better product. I didn't get a purchase link for it in these results.
- **Heat and UPS caveats.** Output drops to 1,500 W in 95-104°F heat. The UPS function can fail if the "Grid Enhancement" app setting is on ([Best Batteries](https://us.best-batteries.com/reviews/bluetti-ac180/)).

**Where to buy**
- **BLUETTI AC180 (official US store, $499):** https://www.bluettipower.com/products/ac180?variant=44099774480603. Check that you're getting the standalone unit and not a solar bundle.
- **Cheaper alternative, ALLPOWERS P1800:** 1,024 Wh, 1,800 W, about $395 with code ALLPOWERS26. The warranty is shorter at 24 months, and the cycle life is rated to 70% rather than 80%. This is an affiliate link: https://dealectric.com/go/allpowers-p1800-1024wh

**Bottom line:** Buy the AC180 if you can get it at $449 or less, or if you want a proven unit for AC loads. If you'll carry it a lot or run small loads for hours, look at the Elite 100 V2 or the Anker Solix C1000 Gen 2, which OutdoorGearLab prefers.
